nameStory: The Eastern Whip-poor-will gets its name from its distinctive call that sounds exactly like someone shouting "whip-poor-WILL! whip-poor-WILL!" over and over again. This is called onomatopoeia - when a word imitates the sound it describes, just like "buzz" or "crash." You'll also hear people call it "whip-o-will" or other variations, but they're all trying to capture that unmistakable three-note song.
description: The Eastern Whip-poor-will is a medium-sized bird about the size of a robin, measuring 8-11 inches long. It belongs to the nightjar family - birds specially designed for nighttime hunting with huge mouths for catching insects on the wing. These birds are masters of camouflage, with mottled brown, gray, and buff feathers that make them nearly invisible when resting on dead leaves or tree bark during the day. You're much more likely to hear a whip-poor-will than see one, as they're active at dusk and dawn when most of us aren't out birding.

idTips.label: Distinctive Call
idTips.description: The unmistakable "whip-poor-WILL!" call repeated rapidly, sometimes hundreds of times in a row. Listen for the emphasis on the third syllable, like someone urgently calling Will's name.

idTips.label: Camouflaged Plumage
idTips.description: Intricate pattern of browns, grays, and buffs that looks exactly like dead leaves and bark. The feathers have a soft, almost velvety texture when seen up close.

idTips.label: Huge Mouth
idTips.description: Enormous gape surrounded by bristles that acts like a bug-catching net. The mouth opens wider than seems possible for the bird's head size.

idTips.label: Ground-resting Behavior
idTips.description: Sits motionless on the ground or low branches during the day, often lengthwise along a branch rather than perched across it like most birds.

idTips.label: Large Dark Eyes
idTips.description: Prominent dark eyes that reflect light at night, giving them an almost owl-like appearance in flashlight beams.

idTips.label: Short Legs and Bill
idTips.description: Tiny legs and a small, weak-looking bill that seems inadequate for the bird's size - these are signs of an aerial insect hunter.

habitat: Eastern Whip-poor-wills prefer open woodlands and forest edges throughout New England, especially areas where forests meet fields, clearings, or old logging roads. They need a mix of trees for daytime roosting and open spaces for nighttime insect hunting. You'll often find them in oak-pine forests, abandoned farmland growing back to forest, and suburban areas with large wooded lots.

seasonality.spring: Arrive in late April to early May and immediately begin their famous calling, especially on warm, moonlit nights. This is peak time to hear them as males establish territories and attract mates.
seasonality.summer: Calling continues through breeding season but may decrease during nesting. Look for them resting on the ground in dappled shade during hot days, perfectly camouflaged among leaf litter.
seasonality.fall: Calling becomes sporadic as they prepare for migration. Most birds depart by September, though you might hear occasional calls on warm October evenings.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England - these insect-eaters migrate to Central America and northern South America where flying insects remain abundant year-round.

funFact: A male whip-poor-will holds the world record for most consecutive calls by any bird - one individual was recorded calling "whip-poor-will" 1,088 times in a row without stopping, which would take about 20 minutes of non-stop shouting!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with owls due to their nocturnal habits and large eyes, but whip-poor-wills have tiny bills and catch insects on the wing rather than hunting small mammals. Remember: if you hear "who-who-who," it's an owl; if you hear "whip-poor-WILL," you've found your nightjar.
contextualKnowledge: Many people know the whip-poor-will from folklore and literature rather than real-life encounters - it's become a symbol of wild, lonely places in American culture. The bird appears in countless poems and songs as the voice of the wilderness, though habitat loss means fewer people actually hear them today than in past generations.
compareHints: Eastern Whip-poor-will's closest relative in our region is the Chuck-will's-widow, but that species barely reaches southern New England and has a different call that sounds like "chuck-will's-WID-ow." Chuck-will's-widows are also noticeably larger and prefer more southern, warmer climates. The whip-poor-will is the nightjar you'll encounter throughout most of New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to their close relative the Eastern Whip-poor-will, chuck-will's-widow are significantly larger and bulkier with a slower, more measured call rhythm.
